reconstruction.what_the_paper_does: A measurement+method paper on a failure mode in a single-node, local-first agent memory system (MemTether): retrievers cannot distinguish facts ABOUT a query entity from facts that merely CONTAIN the query string. It quantifies this on 10 queries (baseline precision@10 = 28%), identifies two root causes (use_count popularity ranking; regex-based entity extraction with 58.1% coverage), and proposes entity-aware hybrid retrieval: subject-proximity scoring (char-position thresholds 30/80/200) gated on entity-index coverage (>=3 facts with ss>=0.7), improving precision@10 to 73%.

architectural_footprint.storage: One shared SQLite file: facts, fact_entities (21,300 links / 7,413 distinct entities), embeddings + FTS5 with RRF fusion, use_count counters, Q-values. 15 AI clients, 2,378 writes over 30 days, 1,975 active memories.
architectural_footprint.concurrency: 15 concurrent clients on one SQLite file; journal mode, busy_timeout, transaction scope never stated. use_count increments are read-modify-write — the exact field the paper shows drives the ranking failure.
architectural_footprint.scoring_layer: Deterministic char-position heuristic (ss in {1.0,0.7,0.5,0.3,0.1}) blended 0.7*ss + 0.2*q + 0.1*uc, with a coverage gate and baseline fallback.

central_claims: C2: Entity-aware hybrid improves to 73/100 (+45pp), improvement in 7/10 queries, one regression (temporal accuracy 1->0).
C3: Two independent root causes: popularity ranking and regex extraction coverage (58.1%).
C4: The subject-proximity method generalizes as post-processing on any retriever (no language-specific parsing).

findings.issue: Table caption admits the headline 28/100 is not reproducible from the table: per-run rows sum to 19/100, and 9 pairs come from an undisclosed 'second evaluation pass'
findings.relevant_text: The 9-count discrepancy between the 28/100 headline and the 19/100 per-run sum arises because the headline includes 9 additional query-result pairs from a second evaluation pass not shown in this per-query breakdown.
findings.concern: A precision@10 benchmark has exactly 100 labeled pairs; there is no legitimate 'second pass not shown'. Either (a) the two methods were evaluated on different result sets (baseline ran twice on supersession/fuseeval, entity-aware once, or vice versa), making the comparison mismatched; or (b) the 28/100 number came from a different labeling snapshot than the table. Worse, Table tab:baseline contains duplicated queries (supersession 0/10 and 2/10; fuseeval 2/10 and 2/10) with the note 'run twice to verify stability' — supersession swung 0/10 -> 2/10 between reruns, i.e., the baseline retrieval is nondeterministic by at least ±2/10 per query, and the reported numbers may cherry-pick reruns. If baseline precision has ±20% run-to-run variance per query, the +45pp aggregate claim needs rerun-level reporting, not a single pass.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: The caption is an honest disclosure; the second pass was the complete evaluation and the table is an illustrative subset. Embedding-model or FTS ordering differences explain the supersession rerun variance.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Honest disclosure of an unexplained discrepancy is not reconciliation. The reader cannot reconstruct which 100 pairs produced 28/100 vs 73/100, cannot tell whether the two methods saw the same candidate sets, and the caption itself documents nondeterminism large enough (2/10 per query) to matter at n=10. This is the central quantitative claim of the paper.
findings.suggestions: Publish the exact 100 (query, result, label) rows for both methods; state why two passes exist and which pass Table tab:results reports; if retrieval is nondeterministic, report mean±range over reruns per query and per method; remove or explain the duplicated rows rather than labeling them 'stability verification'.

findings.issue: Ground-truth rule is partly circular: 'ABOUT iff query is substring of the fact's primary entity (the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor)' uses the same extraction machinery whose failure is the paper's Cause 2
findings.relevant_text: a pair is labeled ABOUT if the query string appears as a substring of the fact's primary entity (the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor) ... determined by manual inspection of each fact content.
findings.concern: The labeling rule delegates to 'the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor' — but the paper's own finding is that this extractor covers only 58.1% of facts and misses English multi-word terms entirely. For facts with no entity link, the rule is undefined; 'manual inspection' is asserted to cover these cases but no inter-rater agreement, labeler identity (authors vs independent), or adjudication procedure is reported. Since the proposed method's score (ss) is also a function of entity position in content, labels derived from entity extraction correlate mechanically with the method's score: queries where extraction works get both ABOUT labels and high ss; queries where extraction fails get neither. The +45pp improvement may partly measure 'extraction succeeds' rather than 'retrieval is about-correct'. The temporal accuracy regression (1->0) is one visible instance: extraction fails, no entity link, label collapses.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: The rule is explicitly stated to be independent of the retrieval methods and labels are manually verified by inspection; the fallback cases (no entity link) are handled by inspection, not by the extractor.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Independence from 'retrieval methods' is not independence from the entity index, which is shared infrastructure between label rule and method. Manual inspection with no protocol, no second rater, and no kappa on 100 subjective pairs is exactly the setup where the labeling drifts toward the proposed method's inductive bias.
findings.suggestions: Define ABOUT purely by human judgment with a written rubric (e.g., 'would a user asking about X consider this fact primarily informative about X?'), have two labelers with reported agreement, and release the labels. Show that the improvement survives on the subset of queries where entity extraction succeeded (it does: packy, memory_hub, fuseeval) — i.e., decompose the +45pp into 'extraction-fix effect' vs 'ranking-fix effect'.

findings.issue: Concurrency model still unspecified; now load-bearing because the paper's Cause 1 is precisely the use_count field, which is a read-modify-write counter under 15 concurrent clients
findings.relevant_text: the baseline ranks them by use_count (retrieval frequency). This surfaces high-traffic facts regardless of relevance.
findings.concern: This paper's root-cause analysis elevates use_count from a passive statistic to the villain of the story: the top-5 'packy' facts ranked by use_count (40, 37, 31, 27, 26) are all mention-only. But use_count is incremented on retrieval by 15 concurrent clients against one SQLite file; the paper never states journal mode, busy_timeout, or whether increments are transactional. If increments are lost under contention (SQLITE_BUSY, non-atomic read-modify-write), the popularity signal is biased toward whichever clients' writes survived — the paper cannot distinguish 'popularity ranking is wrong' from 'popularity ranking is computed over a corrupted popularity signal'. The architectural claim 'popularity-based ranking is a root cause' requires the popularity data to be trustworthy.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: 77 writes/day is low contention; use_count corruption would be small relative to the qualitative pattern (mention-only facts at the top), and the fix (subject proximity) does not depend on use_count being exact.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Retrieval events (which bump use_count) are not the same as the 77 writes/day; retrieval frequency is the whole point of the counter and is unmeasured/undisclosed in this paper. Burst concurrency from 15 clients is unbounded by daily averages, as before. The paper should at least state that use_count increments are single-statement UPDATEs (atomic in SQLite) or report the locking configuration.
findings.suggestions: State journal mode (WAL?), busy_timeout, and whether use_count increments use atomic UPDATE ... SET use_count = use_count + 1; report any lock errors in the window; if available, cross-check use_count totals against retrieval-request logs.
findings.status: escalated-from-E1-01 (adapted: concern now attaches to the popularity-ranking root cause rather than dead-rate measurement)

findings.issue: Entity-index consistency and transaction boundaries: 827/1,975 active facts have no entity link, but the paper never says whether that is extraction failure or a torn fact/fact_entities write
findings.relevant_text: This misses 41.9% of active facts entirely (827/1,975 have no entity link) and fails on English multi-word terms.
findings.concern: The 41.9% coverage gap is attributed entirely to regex limitations, but architecturally there are two ways a fact lacks an entity link: (a) the extractor ran and found nothing; (b) the fact was written without the fact_entities rows (crash mid-transaction, extraction skipped on a code path, extraction run before/after edit). These have different fixes (better extraction vs guaranteed extraction-at-write). The 'enhanced' extractor adds 4,136 new links to those 827 facts — 5.0 links/fact for facts that supposedly matched no pattern — which suggests either the new patterns are extremely loose or the original extraction never ran on some of these facts. No integrity check (e.g., 'extraction_ran' flag, or re-running the original extractor and counting true zeros) distinguishes the cases.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: The paper documents which queries the extractor fails on (Memory Court 4.7%, temporal accuracy 0%) — this is clearly pattern-miss, not missing writes; and 4,136 links from 4 patterns over 827 facts (~5/fact) is plausible for multi-entity facts.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Query-level coverage stats show pattern failure exists, not that it explains all 827; and 5 links/fact from patterns 'acronyms' and 'file names' would generate enormous noise (every file path becomes an entity), which itself threatens the precision claims if the enhanced index were used at retrieval time. The paper leaves the enhanced index's retrieval impact at 'neutral net effect' without per-query detail.
findings.suggestions: Add a provenance flag or re-extraction audit distinguishing 'extractor ran, zero matches' from 'extraction never ran'; report precision impact of the enhanced index per query, not just aggregate; consider entity quality thresholds given 5 links/fact suggests over-extraction.

findings.issue: Character-position thresholds (30/80/200) are undefined for mixed Chinese/English content and appear tuned on the same queries used for evaluation
findings.relevant_text: idx(e, c) <= 30 (subject) ... <= 80 (prominent) ... <= 200 (mid-text) ... where idx(e,c) is the character position of entity e in content c.
findings.concern: (a) Unit ambiguity: 'character position' in Python (code points) vs SQLite LENGTH (bytes under UTF-8) differ 3x for Chinese text, which dominates the corpus; idx=63 for the parenthetical 'packy' in Table tab:popularity lands in different ss buckets depending on unit. The scoring function is thus not portable between the SQL layer and the Python layer, and the paper doesn't say where it's computed. (b) The thresholds 30/80/200, the gate '>=3 facts with ss>=0.7', and the blend weights 0.7/0.2/0.1 are all unjustified constants selected on — presumably — the same 10 queries that constitute the evaluation. With n=10, tuning five constants on the test set can easily account for a large fraction of +45pp. The generalizability paragraph ('can be applied as a post-processing step on any existing retriever') is unsupported without held-out queries.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: Thresholds are intuitive (subject-initial position), the method is deliberately simple and deterministic, and the fallback gate ensures no harm when they misfire; sensitivity analysis is reasonable future work.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Intuitive constants evaluated on 10 queries with documented nondeterminism (E1-N01) and a partially circular labeling rule (E1-N02) stack three layers of optimistic bias on the headline number. At minimum a threshold-sensitivity table and a disjoint validation set of queries are cheap here.
findings.suggestions: State the unit and computation layer for idx; report precision@10 under threshold perturbation (e.g., 20/50/100, 50/120/300) and weight perturbation; hold out 5-10 additional queries selected before tuning; release the 100 labeled pairs so others can re-tune.

findings.issue: Scaling behavior of the entity-first path is unanalyzed: gate requires scanning entity index for >=3 facts with ss>=0.7, and ss is computed at query time over content
findings.relevant_text: IF entity index has >= 3 facts with ss >= 0.7 THEN return entity-ranked results (subject-proximity order)
findings.concern: Nothing states whether ss is precomputed per (fact, entity) pair or computed per query by scanning content. If per query, cost is O(|facts linked to entity| * |content|) substring search per retrieval — fine at 1,975 facts, but the generalizability claim targets 'any existing retriever', where entity-linked fact sets can be orders of magnitude larger. Latency numbers are absent entirely (the companion paper's B1 gate reported p50=0.037ms; nothing here). The storage schema implication — whether idx/ss is materialized in fact_entities or recomputed — is a schema design decision the paper doesn't discuss.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: At production scale (1,975 facts, max ~dozens of facts per entity) any implementation is fast; premature optimization is out of scope for a failure-mode paper.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Acceptable for the measured system, but the generalizability claim then needs scoping, and a one-line latency measurement would have cost nothing.
findings.suggestions: Report retrieval latency for baseline vs entity-aware on the production DB; state whether ss is precomputed; scope the generalizability claim or note the index-size regime where per-query scanning breaks down.

findings.issue: 30-day window arithmetic and date consistency (prior E1-04 family) partially persists: abstract says 30-day, setting says 2026-09-13 to 2026-10-14 'at time of writing'
findings.relevant_text: During the 30-day study period (2026-09-13 to 2026-10-14 (at time of writing))
findings.concern: Sep 13 to Oct 14 is 31 days; 'at time of writing' inside a date range signals data collection was ongoing when drafted, meaning counts (1,975 active, 2,378 writes, 21,300 links) may be snapshots at different times — especially problematic since the evaluation queries facts whose use_count changes over time. A fixed analysis_date is never stated.
findings.suggestions: State a single analysis_date; unify on 31 days (or true span); give all counts as of that date.
findings.status: escalated-from-E1-04 (residual; the write-governance-specific 12-15% vs 17.9% inconsistency is N/A here)

findings.issue: Durability of the single evidentiary SQLite file remains unaddressed (prior E1-05), now with an added wrinkle: the artifact URL changed to a personal-looking repo (lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact) with no tag/SHA
findings.relevant_text: All measurements are reproducible from the production SQLite database. The evaluation script and retrieval implementation are available at https://github.com/lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact
findings.concern: The DB itself is not released (privacy, per SECURITY.md), so 'reproducible' again means three commands the reader cannot run against the real data. The repository pointer has no commit SHA, tag, or release, and the repo name ('cac-artifact') differs from the project name (MemTether), suggesting an anonymization shim whose persistence is uncertain. The reproducibility commands themselves are inconsistent with the paper's own disclosure: 'Expected: 10/10 ABOUT' for packy under hybrid mode, but if retrieval is nondeterministic (E1-N01's supersession 0->2 rerun), expected values are not stable.
findings.suggestions: Pin a SHA/tag; state integrity_check result and journal mode for the production DB (one paragraph, per prior E1-05); release the 100 labeled pairs and evaluation script version; soften 'Expected: 10/10' to a range if nondeterminism exists.

claim_evidence_gaps: C1 (28% baseline): caption admits 19/100 from shown rows; 9 pairs from undisclosed second pass; duplicated queries with divergent results (supersession 0 vs 2) indicate nondeterminism. Gap: the headline number is not derivable from anything in the paper.

C2 (73%, +45pp): no per-query entity-aware breakdown table (only baseline is tabulated); the sentence listing improvements (packy 1->10, memory_hub 2->10, fuseeval 2->10, Memory Court 1->10) accounts for 40 gained pairs, but Memory Court appears in neither Table tab:baseline's query list nor is it among the '8 distinct query terms' — a ninth query appears in the analysis but not the benchmark table. This is a second, unreconciled composition inconsistency.

C3 (root causes independent): no ablation showing ranking-fix alone vs extraction-fix alone; the enhanced-extractor paragraph says aggregate stays 73% with offsetting effects, which contradicts 'independent root causes' — causes that offset are interacting, not independent.
C4 (generalizability): zero evidence beyond the assertion; method tuned on 10 queries from one deployment.
statistical_issues: n=10 queries, no CIs (paper acknowledges); but additionally baseline nondeterminism ±2/10 per query documented in the paper's own table.
Test-set tuning: thresholds 30/80/200, gate >=3, weights 0.7/0.2/0.1 with no held-out validation.
Ground truth: single manual labeler (apparently), no agreement stats, partial circularity with entity extractor.
The 'consistent across 7 of 10 queries' framing counts duplicated rerun rows as queries (10 rows, 8 distinct terms).
logical_leaps: 'Independent root causes' asserted while the enhanced-extractor experiment shows the two causes offset each other (gains erased by temporal-accuracy regression).

'Guarantees no regression' (Sec 4.2) contradicted within two pages by the temporal accuracy 1->0 regression — the gate guarantees no regression only when extraction failure correlates with fallback correctness, which it didn't.
Generalizability to 'any existing retriever' from a method whose label rule and scoring both depend on the same entity index.
alternative_explanations: The +45pp may largely reflect labeling/measurement artifacts: labels derived from the same entity index the method exploits, nondeterministic baseline cherry-stabilized, and constants tuned on the test set. A skeptical prior: true improvement is real on packy-like queries (where the effect is 1->10, hard to fake) but the aggregate is inflated by 10-20pp.

The popularity-ranking 'root cause' may partly be a use_count-integrity artifact (concurrent increments, E1-N03) — mention-only facts accumulate use_count precisely because they're returned at top, a feedback loop the paper never models (rich-get-richer in the counter it blames).
41.9% no-link rate may include extraction-never-ran facts, not just pattern misses (E1-N04).

gaming_detection.note: Concerning pattern: five free constants tuned on the 10-query test set; a labeling rule correlated with the method's own index; duplicated reruns labeled 'stability verification' while showing a 0->2 swing; and a second evaluation pass contributing 9 pairs that appear only in the headline. Mitigating: the paper does disclose the 19-vs-28 discrepancy in the caption and admits the temporal regression — honest disclosure of weaknesses, but the disclosures reveal problems rather than resolve them. Not fabricated, but the evaluation pipeline is assembled to maximize the headline delta within disclosure boundaries.

closest_prior: mem0 (arXiv:2504.19413), Zep (arXiv:2501.13956), Letta/MemGPT (arXiv:2310.08560) — cited; none measure about-vs-mention precision in production, so the failure-mode characterization is plausibly novel.

Classical IR: entity-oriented search / entity linking (e.g., EntityRank-style subject-importance features, position-based term-proximity scoring in BM25F/proximity models from the 2000s) — the subject-proximity score is a reinvention of position-weighted term scoring, uncited. The claim 'no prior work quantifies the about-vs-mention distinction in agent memory' is plausible; the implicit novelty of position-based scoring is not novel in IR generally.
The companion write-governance paper (cross-referenced as [aoc]/[5] in prior reviews) — this is that paper's retrieval counterpart; the about-vs-mention measurement is the genuinely new piece here.
novelty_check.assessment: Moderate novelty: failure-mode quantification in production agent memory is fresh; the method is a simple, well-precedented heuristic; the paper over-claims generalizability relative to evidence.
novelty_check.search_description: No systematic search described; 'to our knowledge' claim unsupported by any stated methodology (echoes prior E1-06 concern pattern).

data.meta_note: Reconciliation of prior findings: the previous review round targeted the companion write-governance paper (MemTether write efficiency). This submission is the entity-aware retrieval companion paper. E1-02 (3,980-char injection bottleneck) and E4-03/E4-04/E4-06 (gate net-effects, buffer-pool framing, B1 gate) are REFUTED-N/A for this paper (content absent). E1-01 (concurrency) persists in adapted form as E1-N03 — now load-bearing on use_count rather than dead-rate. E1-04 persists residually as E1-N07 (30 vs 31 days; missing analysis_date). E1-05/E2-09 (durability, unpinned artifact) persist as E1-N08. E1-03/E3-04/E3-05 arithmetic errors are N/A here but the same class of error recurs (E1-N01: 19 vs 28). E2-07 (character-unit ambiguity) recurs in new form in E1-N05 (idx unit for Chinese text). The dominant new finding is E1-N01: the paper's own table caption discloses that its headline number cannot be reconstructed from the paper, compounded by a ninth query (Memory Court) appearing in the analysis but not the benchmark. Overall 5: below CCF-C bar as written (unreproducible headline + circular-leaning labels), but the packy-level effect (1->10) and honest disclosure suggest a real phenomenon underneath; fixes are cheap (release labels, per-query table, sensitivity analysis) and would move this to 6-7.

claimed_contribution: Quantify the about-vs-mention failure in a production agent memory: baseline precision@10 = 28% across 10 query terms
Identify two root causes: popularity-based ranking (use_count) and regex-based entity extraction (58.1% coverage)
Propose entity-aware hybrid retrieval with subject-proximity scoring, improving precision@10 to 73% (+45pp)
evidence_markers: Production deployment: 1,975 active memories, 15 AI clients, 30-day window (2026-09-13 to 2026-10-14)
Table 1: per-query baseline precision@10 with dominant failure mode annotations
Table 2: top-5 entity-linked facts for 'packy' showing all 5 are non-about
Table 3: entity extraction coverage by query term (90.5% / 18.1% / 4.7% / 0.0%)
Finding box: 4 query-level improvements (packy 1→10, memory_hub 2→10, fuseeval 2→10, Memory Court 1→10) + 1 regression (temporal accuracy 1→0)
reconstruction.method_summary: Subject-proximity score ss(c,e) ∈ {1.0, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1} based on character index of entity in content; hybrid gating: if ≥3 facts have ss ≥ 0.7 in entity index, return entity-ranked results; else fall back to baseline hybrid search. Final score = 0.7·ss + 0.2·q + 0.1·min(uc,100)/100.
reconstruction.key_artifact_claim: Source at https://github.com/lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact with `python entity_aware_retrieval.py --query ... --mode ...` CLI; SQL reproducible via provided sqlite3 query
reconstruction.implied_user: Local-first solo operator with mixed Chinese/English facts, multi-client agent fleet (15 clients)

findings.issue: `pip install` installability is not advertised — reproducibility points to a raw GitHub URL and a script, not an installable package
findings.relevant_text:
The evaluation script and retrieval implementation are available at https://github.com/lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact
python entity_aware_retrieval.py --query "packy" --mode baseline
findings.concern: The paper's E2 lens expects `pip install <name>` to work and first-run to produce sensible output. This paper does not even advertise a PyPI package; it points to a GitHub repo with a script. A reviewer running `git clone <url> && cd repo && python entity_aware_retrieval.py --query "packy"` will encounter: (1) no requirements.txt mentioned anywhere in the paper; (2) no CLAUDE.md or README excerpt confirming Python version; (3) no assurance that the script's `entity_aware_retrieval.py` entry point actually exists at that path; (4) no path to a `memory.db` fixture — the script is presumed to point at the production DB which is explicitly gitignored per SECURITY.md. The first-run error path is opaque.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: The repo is at the advertised URL and a developer can clone and inspect before running.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: Inspection is not reproduction. Without a pinned version, a lockfile, a minimal fixture DB, and a one-line install command, the reproducibility claim is decorative. SECURITY.md elsewhere in the paper bundle confirms `memory.db` is gitignored — meaning the commands in the Reproducibility section will execute against a non-existent file on a fresh clone.
findings.suggestions: (a) Add a `pip install -e .` or `pip install git+https://github.com/lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact@v1.0` line at the top of Reproducibility. (b) Ship a `tests/fixtures/memory_fixtures.db` (or a `python -m cac_artifact.synthesize --seed 42 --days 30` generator) so the three commands produce non-zero output on a fresh clone. (c) Pin Python version, sentence-transformers/transformers version, and SQLite version in a `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`. (d) Add a `memtether doctor` or `python entity_aware_retrieval.py selfcheck` first-run smoke test that prints dependency versions, SQLite FTS5 availability, and a hello-world round-trip.

findings.issue: The Reproducibility SQL query references a `facts` table with a `uid` column and a `fact_entities` table with `fact_uid`/`uid` columns — but the schema is never published
findings.relevant_text:
sqlite3 memory.db "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM facts f WHERE status='active'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM fact_entities fe WHERE fe.fact_uid = f.uid)"
# Expected: 827 (41.9% of 1975 active)
findings.concern: Every table and column name in the query (`facts`, `fact_entities`, `status`, `uid`, `fact_uid`) is unstated in the paper. The paper says facts are 'linked to zero or more named entities via a fact_entities index table (21,300 links, 7,413 distinct entities)' but never pins primary keys, column types, or whether `facts.uid` exists vs `facts.id` vs `(facts.id, facts.source)`. A reviewer attempting to reproduce either gets 'no such table' (cryptic, no fix path) or runs the query against a schema they guessed and gets a different number silently. This is the primary blocking failure for E2 — without schema documentation, the SQL command cannot be evaluated by a new user.
findings.suggestions: Publish the schema DDL either inline in a 'Schema' subsection or as `docs/schema.sql` linked from the Reproducibility section. The minimum needed: CREATE TABLE statements for `facts`, `fact_entities`, and any auxiliary tables (`audit_log`, `fact_sources`) with column types and primary keys. Alternatively, add a `python entity_aware_retrieval.py --export-schema` CLI flag that dumps the live schema to stdout — this doubles as a smoke test (proves the package installed) and a self-documenting reference.

findings.issue: Subject-proximity score thresholds (30, 80, 200 characters) are not motivated and not exposed as configuration — impossible to tune or audit
findings.relevant_text: ss(c,e) = 1.0 if idx(e,c) ≤ 30 (subject); 0.7 if idx(e,c) ≤ 80 (prominent); 0.5 if count(e,c) ≥ 2 (repeated); 0.3 if idx(e,c) ≤ 200 (mid-text); 0.1 otherwise (passing reference)
findings.concern: The five-tier ladder is the paper's core methodological contribution. A reviewer cannot: (a) reproduce the score for a given fact because the thresholds are baked into code without documentation; (b) understand how thresholds interact with the Chinese-character density (which the paper does not address — Chinese characters are 3 bytes in UTF-8 but 1 character in SQLite LENGTH() under default collation, making 'idx ≤ 30' mean different things across languages); (c) tune them for their own corpus. The scoring equation is in the paper but the implementation is a black box. This is the opposite of API-ergonomic: the user has no knobs, no schema, and no error messages.
findings.suggestions: Expose thresholds as config keys (e.g., `cac.sp.threshold_subject=30`, `cac.sp.threshold_prominent=80`, `cac.sp.threshold_mid=200`) in a YAML/TOML config or CLI flags (`--sp-threshold-subject 30`). Add a `python entity_aware_retrieval.py --explain-score <fact-id> --query <entity>` command that prints ss(q,f), q, uc, and the final score for a single fact, so a reviewer can audit any decision without re-running the full benchmark. Document the byte-vs-grapheme unit choice (see E2-N07).

findings.issue: Ground-truth labeling procedure is described as 'independent' but the rule is self-contradictory ('primary entity' + 'substring of the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor')
findings.relevant_text: a pair is labeled about if the query string appears as a substring of the fact's primary entity (the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor), and not-about otherwise. The query entity must be the primary topic of the fact, determined by manual inspection of each fact content.
findings.concern: The procedure mixes two definitions: (a) automatic rule: substring-of-first-extracted-entity; (b) manual rule: 'primary topic by manual inspection'. The two can disagree — a fact where 'packy' is the first extracted entity but the content is about something else, or vice versa. The 28/100 baseline score depends on which rule was applied. A reviewer cannot reproduce the ground truth because the procedure's tie-breaker is unspecified. This is an API/ergonomics issue because the paper's central claim (precision 28% → 73%) is computed against this ground truth, but a new user applying the same labeling rule will get different counts.
findings.suggestions: Pick one: either pure substring-of-primary-entity (fully reproducible, no manual step) or pure manual labeling (release the per-query-per-fact labels). Publish the 100 ground-truth labels as `benchmarks/ground_truth.csv` with columns (query, fact_uid, label, labeler, label_method) so reviewers can audit. If manual inspection is the source of truth, state that the substring rule is a fallback approximation, not the actual procedure.

findings.issue: First-run diagnostic absent for 'the script silently returns the wrong number because my fixture has different statistics'
findings.relevant_text: All measurements are reproducible from the production SQLite database
findings.concern: The Reproducibility section gives three commands but no baseline expectations beyond 'Expected: 1/10 ABOUT' and 'Expected: 827'. A first-time user cloning the repo, generating a synthetic fixture (if such a thing existed), and executing the precision@10 benchmark gets one of three failure patterns: (a) ImportError (missing sentence-transformers / faiss / rank_bm25) with no remediation hint; (b) RuntimeError (FTS5 not compiled into system SQLite — common on macOS Python.org builds vs Homebrew) with no fallback to plain FTS4; (c) Successful run with unexpected numbers because the user's data distribution differs from the paper's. None of these have actionable error messages in the paper or (presumably) in the script.
findings.suggestions: Add a one-page first-run recipe: (1) `git clone ... && cd ... && pip install -e .`; (2) `python -m cac_artifact.synthesize --seed 42 --days 30 --out fixtures/memory.db` to create a deterministic 30-day fixture; (3) `python entity_aware_retrieval.py selfcheck --db fixtures/memory.db` which prints: Python version, SQLite version, FTS5 availability, embedding model loaded, expected-vs-actual for the three paper commands. If any check fails, print a structured remediation message ('Install FTS5: brew install sqlite3 or use the bundled sqlite3-binary package').

findings.issue: API ergonomics of `entity_aware_retrieval.py` CLI are not documented — flags, output format, exit codes, JSON vs text mode all unknown
findings.relevant_text:
python entity_aware_retrieval.py --query "packy" --mode baseline
# Expected: 1/10 ABOUT (manual ground truth)
findings.concern: The paper shows two flags (`--query`, `--mode`) but does not enumerate: (a) what modes exist (baseline? hybrid? entity? subject-proximity?); (b) whether `--mode hybrid` exists or only `baseline` and `entity`; (c) output format (stdout JSON? pretty-printed table? markdown? CSV?); (d) exit codes (0 always? non-zero on empty results?); (e) how to point the script at a non-default DB (`--db path`? env var `MEMTETHER_DB`?); (f) whether the script requires the ground-truth CSV or evaluates against the live DB. For a paper whose contribution is a method, the user-facing surface is the API and it is essentially undocumented.
findings.suggestions: Add a 'CLI Reference' subsection or `docs/cli.md` with: full flag list, output schemas (with one example of each mode), exit-code table, environment variables (MEMTETHER_DB, MEMTETHER_EMBEDDING_MODEL), and a worked example showing both modes for one query. If the tool supports JSON output (`--format json`), show the JSON schema, because that is what automation and reviewers will consume.

findings.subject: Subject-proximity score thresholds (idx ≤ 30, 80, 200) use 'characters' without specifying SQLite LENGTH() vs grapheme vs token, breaking i18n reproducibility
findings.id_continued: carried over from E2-07 family for the entity-aware paper
findings.issue: The 30/80/200-character thresholds behave differently across Chinese (high-density, low grapheme count) and English (low-density, high grapheme count) facts in the same DB
findings.relevant_text: ss(c,e) = 1.0 if idx(e,c) ≤ 30 (subject); 0.7 if idx(e,c) ≤ 80 (prominent); 0.3 if idx(e,c) ≤ 200 (mid-text)
findings.concern: Table 2 shows Chinese facts with `idx=63` (parenthetical) receiving subject-position-class scores despite being parentheticals. This is direct evidence the unitization is miscalibrated for Chinese: 63 characters in Chinese is a much shorter visual span than 63 characters in English, so the 'subject ≤ 30' threshold already classifies many parenthetical mentions as subjects in Chinese facts. The paper does not address this. A reviewer tuning the score on a mixed-language corpus cannot tell whether their Chinese-facts are systematically over-classified as subjects.
findings.suggestions: Specify the unit explicitly: SQLite `LENGTH()` returns characters under UTF-8 (so Chinese = 1 char, English = 1 char regardless of byte count), but visual/linguistic density differs by ~2-3x. Either: (a) report score buckets per-language in a new table; (b) use byte thresholds normalized to a per-fact byte budget (`idx / LENGTH(content) ≤ 0.1`); (c) add a `cac.sp.density_aware=true` config that uses grapheme count from a Unicode-segmentation library.

findings.issue: Examples are incomplete: only the 'packy' query is worked through; the four failed queries (hubguard, supersession, temporal accuracy) and the regression (temporal accuracy 1→0) get no example
findings.relevant_text: Top result is a GUI automation tool whose file path contains 'packy' (Section 2.2); temporal accuracy 1→0 regression in Finding box and Section 5.1
findings.concern: The 'packy' example is well-developed (Table 1 row, Table 2 top-5, Section 2.2 walkthrough). But: (a) hubguard (0/10) and supersession (0/10) — the two worst-performing baseline queries — get zero example, no content excerpt, no entity-index dump. A reader cannot tell whether these are genuine structural impossibilities or labeling artifacts. (b) The temporal accuracy regression is mentioned three times but never explained: why does entity-aware go 1→0? Is it because the entity index lacks 'temporal accuracy' (coverage 0%) AND the hybrid gating mistakenly returns empty when entity count < 3? Without a worked example the regression is a footnote, not a finding. (c) The Finding box claims 'correctly falls back to baseline' for queries where extraction fails — no example confirms this fallback actually produces baseline numbers, not some intermediate degraded behavior.
findings.suggestions: Add a 'Failure-mode walkthrough' subsection with: (1) one full example for hubguard (top-5 with entity-position annotations like Table 2); (2) one full example for temporal accuracy showing the entity-index lookup, the gating decision (count < 3 → fallback), and the post-fallback top-5 — this directly explains the 1→0 regression; (3) one example for Memory Court showing how the enhanced English patterns recover entity links (5→9 per Section 5.1).

findings.issue: Error messages: when the entity-aware method's hybrid gating triggers, the user has no way to inspect why it fell back to baseline
findings.relevant_text: IF entity index has ≥3 facts with ss ≥ 0.7: return entity-ranked results; ELSE return baseline hybrid search
findings.concern: The gating rule is opaque: a developer running the method on a new corpus sees results that look like baseline output but has no signal whether (a) the entity index had <3 high-ss facts (gate triggered), (b) the entity index was empty (different code path?), (c) the gate was bypassed due to a config flag. The paper's 'correctly falls back' claim is unfalsifiable from the CLI alone. For a retrieval system serving 15 clients, a user debugging 'why is this query returning baseline-style results' needs at minimum a trace flag or a structured log line showing the gate's decision.
findings.suggestions: Add a `--verbose` or `--explain-gate` flag that prints `gate_decision: count_in_index=2, threshold=3, fallback_reason='INSUFFICIENT_HIGH_SS'`. Even better, log to stderr in JSON: `{"query": "temporal accuracy", "entity_count": 0, "high_ss_count": 0, "gate_fired": false, "results_source": "baseline"}`. This doubles as debugging output for production agents and as audit trail for reproducibility.

findings.issue: The `use_count` field is referenced as 'popularity (retrieval frequency)' but its update mechanism is never described — does it increment on every retrieval or only on hits within top-k?
findings.relevant_text: Cause 1: Popularity-Based Ranking ... the baseline ranks them by use_count (retrieval frequency). Table 2: top-5 entity-linked facts for 'packy' ranked by use_count.
findings.concern: If `use_count` increments on every retrieval call (even zero-hit queries), it is biased upward by spam. If it only increments on top-k hits, then the popularity signal is curated. If it increments only on ground-truth-relevant retrievals, it is data-leaked. The paper does not say. A reviewer reproducing Table 2's `use_count=40` fact needs to know whether to expect this count after running the retriever once, zero times, or once per successful retrieval. This is API behavior — it determines what `use_count` means to a user.
findings.suggestions: Add one sentence: 'use_count is incremented by 1 each time a fact is returned in the top-k=10 of any retrieval call, regardless of relevance; a fact retrieved 40 times was returned in the top-10 of 40 distinct queries.' If the increment policy is different, state the policy and the rationale.

findings.issue: No version pinning, no CHANGELOG anchor, no commit reference for the artifact — a reviewer cloning six months from now gets a moving target
findings.relevant_text: The evaluation script and retrieval implementation are available at https://github.com/lanbass869-cell/cac-artifact
findings.concern: The Reproducibility section gives a URL but no version tag, no commit SHA, no release artifact (zip/tarball). If the repo evolves (and the SECURITY.md elsewhere in the bundle suggests `v0.1.0a7` is the current line, implying active change), a reviewer cloning `main` six months from now may get a different `--mode` flag, a renamed CLI, or refactored schema. For a paper whose central claim is a +45pp precision improvement, the artifact must be pinned.
findings.suggestions: Add `git checkout <commit-sha>` or `git checkout v1.0` (or `paper-cac-v1` tag) to the Reproducibility section. If the repo does not have tags, create one retroactively at the commit closest to the paper's submission date. Optionally host a Zenodo DOI or a GitHub Release tarball for permanent citation.

findings.issue: The `enhanced index recovers additional entity links` paragraph (Section 5.1) describes an English-pattern augmentation but gives no pattern list, no example, no recall/precision on the added links
findings.relevant_text: We add four deterministic English patterns: (1) multi-word Title Case; (2) acronyms; (3) file names; (4) lowercase technical terms followed by Chinese. Applied to the 827 facts with no entity link, these patterns add 4,136 new entity links.
findings.concern: Four patterns, 4,136 new links — that is an average of 1,034 new links per pattern, which is suspiciously high for 'multi-word Title Case' alone. Without: (a) the actual regex for each pattern, (b) one positive and one false-positive example per pattern, (c) precision estimate for the new links (the paper says Memory Court improved 5→9 and supersession 0→2, but does not say what fraction of the 4,136 new links are spurious), the 'enhanced index' claim is unfalsifiable. A reviewer cannot even evaluate whether to use the enhancement.
findings.suggestions: Publish the four regex patterns (they are deterministic — no IP reason to withhold). Add a precision sample: 'We manually audited 100 random new links; 87 were correct, 13 were spurious (e.g., date strings mistaken for acronyms). Estimated precision: 87%.' If precision is acceptable, this becomes a positive contribution; if not, the paper should report the failure mode rather than the link count alone.

findings.issue: The 28/100 vs 73/100 numbers include a self-acknowledged counting inconsistency in Table 1
findings.relevant_text: Table 1 caption: 'the full benchmark sums to 28/100 as reported in Table 4; the per-run counts in this table total 19/100 across 10 rows... The 9-count discrepancy... arises because the headline includes 9 additional query-result pairs from a second evaluation pass not shown in this per-query breakdown.'
findings.concern: The paper openly acknowledges that Table 1 (the per-query breakdown) sums to 19, not 28, and explains the gap as 'a second evaluation pass not shown'. This is a transparency-positive disclosure but a reproducibility-negative signal: a reviewer running the published benchmark will produce 19, not 28, with no path to the missing 9 unless they re-derive the experimental protocol. This is the kind of internal inconsistency that E2-N04 (ground truth), E2-N08 (examples), and E2-N11 (version pin) compound: multiple small reproducibility gaps, each individually minor, jointly prevent a new user from reproducing the headline number.
findings.suggestions: Either: (a) publish the second evaluation pass as a separate query set (e.g., `benchmarks/run1.csv` and `benchmarks/run2.csv`) with the labels for both, so 19+9=28 is computable; or (b) report the headline as 19/N from a single canonical run. The current 'trust me, there is a second pass' framing makes the 28/100 claim dependent on undocumented protocol details.

findings.issue: Related Work paragraph mentions ConflictBank but the paper does not explain why it is a 'different problem' — and ConflictBank could conceivably apply to fact supersession in agent memory
findings.relevant_text: ConflictBank addresses contradiction detection, a different problem.
findings.concern: ConflictBank's remit is 'evaluating the influence of knowledge conflicts in LLM'. This is closer to the paper's subject than the paper acknowledges — knowledge conflicts include 'a fact contradicts another fact', which is exactly the about-vs-mention problem when an LLM retrieves both. One sentence of dismissal without citation-level evidence ('we read ConflictBank §X and it does not address retrieval precision') is insufficient novelty-gating. From an E2 perspective, the related-work gap also means the paper's reproducibility and adoption story is incomplete: a user comparing MemTether's entity-aware retrieval against ConflictBank-style contradiction filtering has no comparison point.
findings.suggestions: Add a sentence explaining what ConflictBank measures (knowledge-conflict influence on QA, not retrieval precision on a personal memory store) and why the about-vs-mention problem is distinct. If ConflictBank does have a retrieval-precision component, cite the specific section and explain why MemTether's subject-proximity score is complementary.

findings.issue: Finding box and Section 5.1 analysis paragraph are near-duplicates (improvements list: packy 1→10, memory_hub 2→10, fuseeval 2→10, Memory Court 1→10)
findings.relevant_text: Finding box: 'packy (1→10), memory_hub (2→10), fuseeval (2→10), Memory Court (1→10)'; Section 5.1 Analysis paragraph repeats the same list verbatim
findings.concern: Same duplication pattern flagged in E2-08 (different paper). For E2 specifically, this duplication signals that the manuscript has not had a final consistency pass, which directly correlates with the kind of incomplete-API-documentation that erodes reviewer trust. If authors did not notice a paragraph appearing twice, what other artifacts (missing CLI flags, undocumented schema columns, unstated ground-truth rule) did they also miss?
findings.suggestions: Collapse the Finding box and the first paragraph of Section 5.1 Analysis into one location. Run a final `latexdiff` or visual diff before submission. Move the explanatory material (regression, fallback, enhanced index) to a dedicated 'Analysis' subsection rather than having it twice.

statistical_issues: n=10 queries is acknowledged in the paper as too small for significance testing; the +45pp headline is a raw difference with no CI
Per-query improvements are reported as point estimates with no variance; supersession and fuseeval were each run twice for stability but no inter-run variance is reported

Ground-truth labeling is 'manual inspection' (single labeler implied) with no inter-annotator agreement reported — Cohen's kappa or % agreement with a second labeler would be standard for a 100-pair benchmark
No multiple-comparisons correction across the 10 queries; even at n=10 the per-query improvement is suggestive, not confirmatory
logical_leaps: From one worked Chinese example (packy) to the claim 'Our subject-proximity score requires only the fact content and the query string—no language-specific parsing' — the 30/80/200 thresholds implicitly assume Chinese character density (one fact = ~500 Chinese chars in the corpus; idx=63 is mid-fact in Chinese but may be early-fact in English)

From '2 of 10 queries with extraction failure fall back to baseline' to 'This guarantees no regression' — the temporal accuracy 1→0 regression shows it does regress; the claim is internally contradicted

From 'regex extraction is preferred for its determinism and zero cost' to a positive framing of the limitation — determinism is presented as a feature while the paper's own evidence (4 of 4 example queries have 0-90.5% coverage variance) shows it is also the bottleneck

From 'our work is the first to quantify the about-vs-mention distinction' to a positioning of the contribution — no systematic search described (no databases, no keywords, no date range); priority claim unsupported per E1-06 / E2-08 family
alternative_explanations: The 28%→73% improvement could be partly explained by the baseline retriever's use_count ranking (Cause 1), not by subject proximity per se — a baseline retriever that ranked by recency or by inverse use_count might also recover some precision. The paper does not ablate the use_count ranking independently.

The hybrid gating (≥3 high-ss facts) means queries with sparse entity coverage fall back to baseline — the 'no regression' property is partially a definitional artifact of the gating rule, not an empirical finding.

The four English patterns added in Section 5.1 ('enhanced index') may be the actual driver of the +45pp gain on the four improved queries, with the subject-proximity score contributing little; the paper does not ablate the patterns from the score.

evidence: 10-query benchmark is hand-picked to include queries where the entity-aware method is structurally favored (packy, memory_hub, fuseeval, Memory Court all have entity-indexed facts with ss ≥ 0.7) and structurally unfavored queries are partially balanced (CAC 8/10, MEMORY.md 1/10)

Query selection bias: the 10 queries include 8 distinct terms with supersession and fuseeval each run twice — the paper does not state whether the duplicates were added because they were stable or because they boosted the aggregate
Subject-proximity thresholds (30, 80, 200) appear tuned to the paper's own corpus; no held-out validation set is mentioned

The 'second evaluation pass' adding 9 to the headline but not to Table 1 is a minor form of selective reporting — the headline is the maximally favorable count while the per-query breakdown shows the raw distribution
The 73/100 number is presented without negative controls (e.g., 'random baseline precision@10 = 17/100 on the same 10 queries' would show whether 28% is already near random)
