closest_prior_work.name: Zep temporal knowledge graph
closest_prior_work.overlap: Zep's temporal KG also addresses supersession and staleness — it organizes facts by entity and time, which is structurally similar to the paper's entity-aware retrieval. The paper dismisses this with 'use embedding-based retrieval' but Zep's graph traversal is not pure embedding similarity.
closest_prior_work.differentiation: Zep indexes by time and entity but does not explicitly score entity position in fact content (the paper's ss(c,e) is novel). However, the paper does not benchmark against Zep to support this claim.

closest_prior_work.name: Letta/MemGPT
closest_prior_work.overlap: MemGPT's core-memory/archival-memory distinction is itself a form of admission control (what to keep in working memory vs disk). The paper's argument that 'agent memory systems currently admit all writes' is contradicted by MemGPT's explicit paging discipline.
closest_prior_work.differentiation: The paper could distinguish by saying MemGPT does admission at eviction time, not at write time — but it does not.

closest_prior_work.name: mem0
closest_prior_work.overlap: mem0's add/update/search/delete operations include a search-by-entity facility that is conceptually similar to the paper's entity-aware retrieval. No comparison or benchmark against mem0 is provided.

closest_prior_work.name: Open Information Extraction / Subject extraction literature (Hearst 1992, etc.)
closest_prior_work.overlap: The 'is about X' determination via character position is reminiscent of TF-IDF positional weighting (e.g., Wilkinson 1994) and Hearst patterns for hypernym extraction. The subject-proximity score is a simple heuristic that likely has prior art in IR ranking.
closest_prior_work.differentiation: Paper does not cite IR positional weighting literature; novelty over standard IR heuristics not established.

novelty_check.novelty_assessment: The about-vs-mention framing is a familiar IR problem (revisited in TREC 'aboutness' tracks), but its application to agent memory retrieval with the specific hybrid gating rule is plausibly novel in this domain. The paper does not establish novelty against IR literature or against Zep/mem0's entity-retrieval primitives. The +45pp result is reported without comparison to obvious baselines (random, recency, BM25-only).

data.meta_note: This E2 review covers a different paper than the bulk of E1/E2/E3/E4 findings (which address a write-governance/dead-rate paper). Only E2-08 (related-work duplication) and the family E2-09 (no version pin) / E2-11 (ground-truth ambiguity) carry over thematically. The 15 findings here are fresh analysis tailored to this paper's reproducibility, installability, and API-ergonomics gaps. Critical findings cluster around three root failures: (1) no install path is published (paper points to raw URL, not PyPI or pip+git line); (2) no schema is published, so every SQL query is unfalsifiable; (3) no ground-truth labels are published, so the 28%→73% headline is unverifiable. These three together make the paper essentially non-reproducible for a new user. The E2 lens (usability/installability) rates this paper low: even a developer willing to spend an hour cloning and inspecting cannot reach the headline number without undocumented protocol assumptions (the 'second evaluation pass', the substring-vs-manual ground-truth rule, the regex schema for `facts.uid`). Recommended action: minor revision if the artifact is small enough to ship in supplementary, otherwise major revision requiring a `pip install`-able package, a `docs/schema.sql`, a `benchmarks/ground_truth.csv`, and an explicit first-run recipe.

reconstruction.paper: About or Contains? Entity-Aware Retrieval for Agent Memory (companion to write-governance paper)
reconstruction.thesis: Embedding/keyword retrieval cannot distinguish facts ABOUT an entity from facts MERELY CONTAINING it. In one 30-day production deployment (15 clients, ~2K memories), baseline precision@10 is 28%. Root causes: use_count popularity ranking and regex entity extraction (58.1% coverage, Chinese-only). Fix: subject-proximity scoring with hybrid gating (entity-first when ≥3 subject-position facts exist, else baseline fallback), yielding 73% precision@10 (+45pp) on a 10-query manually-labeled benchmark.

findings.issue: Ground-truth labeling is defined two contradictory ways, and the 'independent rule' is circular with the proposed method
findings.relevant_text: a pair is labeled ABOUT if the query string appears as a substring of the fact's primary entity (the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor)... determined by manual inspection... The subject-proximity score ranks facts by the position of the query entity in content.
findings.concern: Section 2.3 first defines ground truth via substring-of-primary-entity (the SAME extractor whose coverage failure Cause 2 diagnoses — labels inherit extractor bias), then says 'the query entity must be the primary topic, determined by manual inspection.' Which was it? If the rule is 'query appears as primary entity / subject position,' it directly measures the mechanism the method optimizes (ss=1.0 for idx≤30 subject position), and the +45pp is partly definitional: the method is being graded against a rubric that encodes 'subject position = ABOUT.' A user of mem0/Zep cannot tell whether the gain is real aboutness or aboutness-by-definition.
findings.suggestions: Report inter-annotator agreement (≥2 labelers, κ) with a written annotation guideline; state whether labels were assigned before or after the method was designed; give 3–5 full labeled examples (fact text, label, rationale) for both ABOUT and NOT-ABOUT.

findings.issue: Query selection bias: the 10-query benchmark is a curated set of the authors' own system's failure cases
findings.relevant_text: The variation is not random: queries whose terms appear as subjects in many facts score high; queries whose terms appear in file paths or passing mentions score zero.
findings.concern: The benchmark queries (packy, hubguard, memory_hub, fuseeval, ...) are the deployment's own observed failures, selected because the baseline fails on them and the entity gate fires. This guarantees headline gain: on queries where extraction fails, the method falls back to baseline (no loss), and on queries selected precisely because subject-position facts exist, it wins. This is the optimal design point of the method's own construction, not a representative workload. Product-positioning claim ('better than mem0/Zep/Letta') cannot follow from a benchmark the competitors never ran and that was chosen to fit the method.
findings.strongest_rebuttal: Diagnosing failures from production and fixing them is legitimate engineering science; the fallback gating ensures the benchmark includes negative cases too.
findings.why_rebuttal_insufficient: It's legitimate as a case study, but the abstract sells +45pp as a generalizable advantage. Report the denominator: how many production queries existed in 30 days, how these 10 were sampled, and what happens on a random sample.
findings.suggestions: Sample queries uniformly (or stratified) from the production query log rather than from known failures; report gains on both the failure-selected set and the random set.

findings.issue: Novelty claim 'no prior work quantifies or addresses about-vs-mention' is contradicted by Zep's design and by decades of IR work
findings.relevant_text: Agent memory systems (mem0, Zep, Letta) use embedding-based retrieval... To our knowledge, no prior work quantifies or addresses the about-vs-mention distinction in agent memory retrieval.
findings.concern: Zep's core mechanism IS entity-centric: its temporal knowledge graph retrieves facts via entity nodes and edges, structurally preferring facts *about* entities over lexical coincidences. mem0 similarly maintains entity/relationship-aware memory during ingestion. Outside agent memory, the aboutness problem is foundational IR: entity-ranking tracks (TREC, DBpedia entity retrieval, ESZS), target-entity identification, and 'aboutness' estimation are a mature literature. The paper's subject-position heuristic is a lightweight re-instantiation of entity-focused retrieval; claiming priority without engaging any of this is a competitive-positioning overreach.
findings.suggestions: Run the about-vs-mention diagnostic ON Zep/mem0 (even a 10-query analog) to substantiate the 'shared failure mode' claim; cite and differentiate entity-ranking IR literature; soften 'no prior work' to 'no prior work in agent-memory production measurement.'

findings.issue: n=10 queries, no significance testing, and no cross-validation of the fitted thresholds
findings.relevant_text: With only 10 queries, statistical significance cannot be reliably assessed; we report the raw counts... improvement direction is consistent across 7 of 10 queries.
findings.concern: A +45pp headline on 100 dependent pairs (10 queries × 10 results, correlated within query) has huge uncertainty; a paired bootstrap over queries would likely give a CI spanning tens of pp. Worse, the scoring weights (0.7/0.2/0.1) and position cutoffs (30/80/200 chars) are hand-set on the same 10 queries used for evaluation — the eval set is also the training set. For a product decision ('switch to this'), the noise floor and overfitting risk dominate.
findings.suggestions: Paired bootstrap or exact permutation over queries for a CI; split query set or use leave-one-query-out for threshold selection; disclose how thresholds were chosen.

findings.issue: Internal contradiction: gating 'guarantees no regression,' yet temporal accuracy regresses 1→0
findings.relevant_text: This guarantees no regression... The only regression is temporal accuracy (1$	o$0), where no entity link exists.
findings.concern: If no entity link exists, the gate should fall back to baseline and return baseline's 1/10. A 1→0 regression under the stated algorithm is impossible unless (a) the gate threshold was met by some spurious facts, (b) the enhanced extractor added a wrong link, or (c) the reported mechanism does not match the evaluated code. Any of these undermines the paper's central safety property (fallback preserves baseline), which is the main switching argument: 'adopt entity-aware retrieval risk-free.'
findings.suggestions: Show the gate decision and top-10 for 'temporal accuracy' under both modes; either fix the claimed fallback logic or explain which mechanism produced the regression.

findings.issue: Table 1 per-query sum is 19/100 but the headline is 28/100, explained away in a caption
findings.relevant_text: the per-run counts in this table total 19/100... the headline includes 9 additional query-result pairs from a second evaluation pass not shown in this per-query breakdown.
findings.concern: A 9-pair discrepancy between the breakdown and the headline, absorbed by an unshown 'second evaluation pass,' means the reported +45pp improvement cannot be reconstructed from the paper's own per-query data. Combined with the duplicated-paragraph problems noted in the companion paper (E1-06/E2-08), this reinforces that headline numbers are not audited against a single computation. Also: per-query baseline counts (packy 1, memory_hub 2) do not sum to 28 with any published rule.
findings.suggestions: Publish the full 28/100 and 73/100 query-level breakdowns as one canonical table; delete the caption apology and make the numbers add up; release the labeled pairs as data.

findings.issue: Generalizability paragraph contradicts the method's language-dependence
findings.relevant_text: Our subject-proximity score requires only the fact content and the query string---no language-specific parsing... It can be applied as a post-processing step on any existing retriever.
findings.concern: Character-position cutoffs (30/80/200 chars) encode assumptions about information density — Chinese packs ~2–3x more semantic content per character than English, so 'idx≤30 = subject' is roughly 'first 1–2 clauses' in Chinese but 'first half-sentence' in English. The paper's own English facts needed four NEW language-specific regex patterns. The subject-proximity score is portable in syntax but not in calibration.
findings.suggestions: Report cutoffs in normalized units (tokens or fraction of length) or validate the same cutoffs on English-only facts; temper the generalizability claim.

findings.issue: Cross-paper inconsistency: 1,975 active memories here vs 1,981 in the companion write-governance paper, same window
findings.relevant_text: 30-day study period (2026-09-13 to 2026-10-14)... 1,975 active memories
findings.concern: Two companion papers reporting on the same production window give different active-memory counts (1,975 vs 1,981). Trivial alone, but both papers' contributions are precise counts from one database; readers cross-reading them cannot tell which snapshot either paper used.
findings.suggestions: State the analysis timestamp and snapshot commit for both papers; reconcile the counts or explain the difference (retirements after companion's snapshot?).

findings.issue: Competitive positioning honesty: the real differentiation vs mem0/Zep is unproven; the honest pitch is 'diagnostic + cheap fix,' not 'better system'
findings.relevant_text: Entity-aware retrieval improves precision@10 from 28\% to 73\%
findings.concern: Answering the three positioning questions directly: (1) Real problem? Yes — about-vs-mention is genuine and under-measured; the 28% baseline precision is a valuable, candid number. (2) Solved better than mem0/Zep/letta? Unknown: no competitor was run on any comparable workload, and Zep's entity-centric KG plausibly mitigates the same failure by design. (3) Who switches, and why? The evidence supports only: 'solo local-first operators with an entity index can add a gating layer at near-zero cost with likely upside on entity-centric queries and bounded downside.' That is a reasonable switch reason for a small segment — but the paper never articulates this segment, and its coverage-dependent gains vanish where the regex extractor fails (58% of facts have no entity link, so the gate rarely fires for exactly the queries extraction misses). The abstract's framing overclaims relative to what a mem0 user could verify.
findings.suggestions: Reposition as: measurement of a failure mode + a zero-cost mitigation for entity-indexed local systems; explicitly name the user (local-first solo operator with heterogeneous agents and an existing entity index); add one instrumented comparison (even 10 queries replayed through mem0 or Zep) to convert positioning into evidence.

claim_evidence_gaps: +45pp headline not reconstructible from per-query table (19 vs 28 discrepancy, E4-12).
'No prior work addresses about-vs-mention' asserted without engaging Zep's entity-centric retrieval or entity-ranking IR (E4-09).
'Guarantees no regression' vs the temporal-accuracy regression (E4-11).
Ground truth defined both as an extraction-based rule and manual inspection; no IAA reported (E4-07).
statistical_issues: n=10 queries, within-query correlation ignored; no CI or paired test despite the paper acknowledging the problem.
Scoring weights and position cutoffs hand-tuned on the same 10 queries used for evaluation.
Improvement 'consistent across 7/10' — 3/10 non-improvements include a regression, so the true direction on unseen queries is uncertain.
logical_leaps: From 'fallback preserves baseline when extraction fails' to 'no regression' — contradicted by temporal accuracy.
From one operator's failure-selected queries to 'the about-vs-mention problem affects any retrieval system' at the claimed magnitude.
From ss≥0.7 gate existence to precision gain — gain requires BOTH gate firing AND subject-proximity ranking matching the labels, and labels may encode the same criterion (circularity).
alternative_explanations: The 28%→73% gain may be largely tautological if ABOUT labels were assigned via subject/primary-entity position — the method optimizes exactly that feature.

Low baseline precision may be dominated by the use_count popularity term and the weak Chinese-only extractor — fixing either alone (e.g., dropping popularity weighting) might recover much of the gain without the entity machinery; no ablation separates ss vs popularity removal.
Embedding 'perfect score 1.00 for a file path' suggests possible embedding-misuse (path string similarity), a deployment bug rather than a fundamental about-vs-mention limit.

gaming_detection.evidence: Benchmark queries are the system's own observed failures (max-favorable selection); ground-truth rule correlates with the method's scoring mechanism (circularity risk); thresholds tuned on the eval set; headline number not reconcilable with the published per-query breakdown; 'no prior work' priority claim made without a search description or engagement with the obvious nearest competitor (Zep's entity-centric KG). The companion-paper discipline of honest negative results is present here in the fallback design, but the evaluation framing is assembled to make the +45pp look as strong as possible.

closest_prior: Zep/Rasmussen et al. 2025 — temporal KG with entity-node-centric retrieval (structurally privileges about-entity facts)
TREC entity ranking / DBpedia entity retrieval tracks — target-entity vs mentioning-doc distinction
Classic IR aboutness estimation and query-focus detection; subject-position/topic-signaling features in query-focused summarization
mem0's entity/relationship-aware memory update pipeline (ingestion-time entity resolution)
novelty_check.verdict: The production measurement of about-vs-mention precision in agent memory is plausibly novel as a *measurement*; the fix (subject-position heuristic + gated hybrid) is a modest engineering combination, not a new mechanism. Priority claim as written is overstated.

data.meta_note: Reconciliation of prior findings: this is the companion retrieval paper, not the write-governance paper, so E1-*/E2-*/E3-* (SQLite concurrency, admission gates, reproducibility matrix) apply to the sibling and are deferred there; two carry over structurally — E4-02 (single-operator user identity, unresolved here too: E4-15) and E1-04/E2-08-style numeric-hygiene problems (recurring here as E4-12, a headline not reconstructible from its own table). The pattern across both papers — correct high-level diagnosis, candid limitations, but unaudited derived numbers, untested competitive claims, and single-operator evidence generalized — is now established and is the main thing standing between this work's genuine problem-finding value and a publishable positioning claim. Verdict on the product question: the about-vs-mention measurement is the real contribution; the fix is cheap and plausibly useful for local-first operators with entity indices, but nothing here yet evidences an advantage over mem0/Zep/Letta — the honest pitch is a diagnostic, and the paper should say so.

cross_challenges.challenge: This finding overstates the problem by claiming the scoring implementation is 'a black box' and 'impossible to... audit'. The full scoring equation — including all five thresholds (30/80/200), all five tier values (1.0/0.7/0.5/0.3/0.1), the tie-in to count(e,c)>=2, and the exact combination weights (0.7*ss + 0.2*q + 0.1*min(uc,100)/100) — is published inline in the Method section. A reviewer can hand-compute ss for any (fact, entity) pair given only the fact content and query string, which the paper itself highlights as a strength: 'Our subject-proximity score requires only the fact content and the query string---no language-specific parsing, no embedding model.' The genuine gaps are narrower than E2 claims: (a) thresholds are not exposed as runtime configuration (a configurability/ergonomics issue, not an auditability one), and (b) the byte-vs-character unit of idx() is unspecified, which matters for the Chinese-heavy corpus. Those warrant a minor/major ergonomics note, not a 'critical' auditability failure. The suggested --explain-score flag is a nice-to-have, not a blocker — the deterministic formula in the paper already permits manual audit.
cross_challenges.evidence: Method section, equation for ss(c,e) with explicit thresholds 30/80/200 and weights 0.7/0.2/0.1; Generalizability paragraph: 'requires only the fact content and the query string---no language-specific parsing, no embedding model. It can be applied as a post-processing step on any existing retriever.'

cross_challenges.challenge: The 'self-contradictory' framing is too strong. The two sentences admit a coherent sequential reading: the fact's primary entity is determined (by manual inspection of content, since the regex extractor's first-entity output is known to be unreliable — Table 3 shows 0-18% coverage on some terms), and the about/not-about label is then assigned by the deterministic substring rule against that primary entity. Under this reading there is no tie-breaker problem because the rules operate on different stages (entity identification vs. label assignment), not as competing definitions of the label. The real defect is underspecification — the paper does not state this ordering explicitly and does not release the 100 labels — which is a documentation gap that one sentence of clarification plus a ground_truth.csv would fix. E2's suggestion to 'pick one' rule is unnecessary; publishing the labels (which E2 also suggests) resolves the issue without changing the procedure. Severity should be minor-to-major documentation, not a threat to the central 28%->73% claim, since the label independence is affirmed ('independent of the retrieval methods being compared and does not rely on character position').
cross_challenges.evidence: Ground Truth section: 'a pair is labeled about if the query string appears as a substring of the fact's primary entity (the first entity extracted by the predicate extractor)... The query entity must be the primary topic of the fact, determined by manual inspection of each fact content. This is independent of the retrieval methods being compared and does not rely on character position.'

data.agreement_note: I fully agree with E2-N01, E2-N02, and E2-N05. E2-N02 is the most damning: the Reproducibility section's SQL query references facts.uid, fact_entities.fact_uid, and status columns whose schema appears nowhere in the paper or the paper bundle, and SECURITY.md confirms memory.db is gitignored, so the three commands cannot execute against any artifact a fresh clone contains — the 'Expected: 827' output is unfalsifiable. E2-N01 correctly identifies that the reproducibility claim is decorative without an install path, pinned dependencies, or a fixture DB; the paper's own SECURITY.md (memory.db excluded from the repo) is direct internal evidence that the advertised commands fail on first run. E2-N05's three failure patterns (ImportError with no remediation, FTS5 availability varying across SQLite builds, silent numeric divergence) are realistic and unaddressed anywhere in the paper. I would add one reinforcement to E2-N02: Table 1 itself contains an internal inconsistency (headline 28/100 vs. per-run sum 19/100, explained only by an unverifiable 'second evaluation pass not shown'), which compounds the schema opacity — a reviewer cannot even reconcile the paper's own tables, let alone reproduce them against a database they cannot obtain.

cross_challenges.challenge: E4-10 overstates a limitation that the paper has already transparently disclosed. The paper states verbatim: 'With only 10 queries, statistical significance cannot be reliably assessed; we report the raw counts and note that the improvement direction is consistent across 7 of 10 queries.' The authors (i) decline to claim statistical significance, (ii) report raw counts rather than inferential statistics, and (iii) flag n=10 as a limitation in the Limitations paragraph. Demanding 'paired bootstrap or exact permutation' as if the paper had concealed this is unfair — they are explicitly presenting a case study, not a significance-tested comparison. The recommendation to use leave-one-query-out for threshold selection is reasonable engineering advice, but characterizing the paper as hiding overfitting risk misreads the Limitations section. A fairer framing: the n=10 issue is real but already author-acknowledged, so the review should focus on whether the disclosed limitation is sufficient for the claims made — not on whether the limitation was hidden.
cross_challenges.evidence: Section 4 opens with: 'With only 10 queries, statistical significance cannot be reliably assessed; we report the raw counts and note that the improvement direction is consistent across 7 of 10 queries.' The Limitations paragraph reiterates: 'Our evaluation uses 10 queries from a single production deployment.' The abstract itself frames this as a production case study, not a controlled benchmark. The paper never claims p-values, CIs, or generalizability beyond the deployment context.

cross_challenges.challenge: E4-09 partially conflates two different claims. The paper claims novelty 'in agent memory retrieval,' not 'in information retrieval generally.' Entity-ranking (TREC, DBpedia) and aboutness literature are well-known, but they target document/entity retrieval over web or Wikipedia corpora — not retrieval over a personal agent's episodic fact store where the 'facts' are short LLM-generated snippets (mean length appears to be <500 chars based on idx values in Table 2). Zep's temporal knowledge graph is cited but the paper's specific claim is that Zep/mem0/Letta have not *quantified* about-vs-mention precision in production. The novelty claim would be more defensibly worded as 'no prior agent-memory production study reports precision@10 broken down by about-vs-mention,' but the 'no prior work addresses' phrasing is overreach. E4-09's core point about Zep being entity-centric is valid, however — the paper should have run a baseline comparison on Zep rather than asserting it shares the failure mode without evidence.
cross_challenges.evidence: Section 6 (Related Work): 'To our knowledge, no prior work quantifies or addresses the about-vs-mention distinction in agent memory retrieval.' The qualifier 'in agent memory retrieval' is present, but the verb 'addresses' is too strong. The paper never engages with Zep's entity-centric design despite citing it, which is a legitimate gap E4-09 correctly identifies.

data.agreement_note: I fully agree with E4-07 (the two ground-truth clauses — substring-of-primary-entity vs. manual inspection of primary topic — are genuinely in tension and need disambiguation; the paper should publish inter-annotator agreement and a labeling guideline), E4-08 (the 10-query benchmark appears curated from the authors' own failure cases with no denominator or random-sample baseline, which is the most consequential threat to external validity in the paper), and especially E4-11 (the temporal accuracy 1→0 regression is a logical contradiction given the stated gate logic: if no entity link exists for 'temporal accuracy' per Table 3, the gate condition (≥3 facts with ss≥0.7) cannot be met, so the fallback should return baseline's 1/10, not 0/10; this either reveals a bug in the evaluated code, a misstated algorithm, or a spurious entity link created by the enhanced extractor — and the paper's central 'no regression' safety claim collapses until this is resolved). I would add one further concern not raised by E4: Table 1 (baseline precision) has an internal arithmetic inconsistency — the caption acknowledges a '9-count discrepancy' between the 28/100 headline and 19/100 per-run sum due to 'a second evaluation pass not shown,' but this undisclosed second pass means the reported baseline number is not reproducible from the table, which is a basic reporting hygiene issue for a paper whose reproducibility section emphasizes exact SQLite queries.

cross_challenges.challenge: I disagree with escalating this to major. The finding is entirely speculative: the paper's claim about use_count is qualitative (mention-only facts with high use_count crowd out subject-position facts), not quantitative. Table tab:popularity shows the top-5 use_count values are 40/37/31/27/26 — a spread of 14 — while the subject-position facts are described as 'buried' far below. Even substantial lost-update corruption would need to reorder facts across this gap to change the conclusion. The proposed method's final score is 0.7·ss + 0.2·q + 0.1·min(uc,100)/100, i.e., use_count contributes at most 0.1 of the score, so the fix's +45pp cannot be an artifact of counter integrity. More importantly, E1-N03's framing ('the paper cannot distinguish popularity ranking is wrong from popularity ranking computed over a corrupted signal') misreads the causal claim: the paper's Cause 1 is that ranking BY popularity is wrong regardless of whether the popularity numbers are exact. Even a perfectly atomic counter would rank the parenthetical 'packy' fact (use_count=40) above 'packy分组机制'. The nondeterminism of supersession reruns (E1-N01) is a retrieval-order issue, not a use_count-write issue. A one-line 'use_count increments are single-statement UPDATEs' clarification would be nice but does not gate any conclusion. Downgrade to minor.
cross_challenges.evidence: Table tab:popularity: use_count 40/37/31/27/26, all mention-only ('idx=63 (parenthetical)', 'idx=54 (tag)', 'idx=288 (list end)'); the about-packy fact 'packy分组机制: 一个key只能调本组模型' has 'lower use_count'. Score formula: score = 0.7·ss + 0.2·q + 0.1·min(uc,100)/100.

cross_challenges.challenge: I agree with the core circularity concern but think 'critical' overstates the impact, for a reason E1 did not check: the paper's own decomposition partially answers it. The Finding 1 paragraph reports per-query deltas — packy 1→10, memory_hub 2→10, fuseeval 2→10, Memory Court 1→10 — and Table tab:coverage shows these are precisely the queries where the entity index had at least some correct links (fuseeval 18.1%, Memory Court 4.7%). The 'extraction-fix effect' E1 asks to isolate is thus visible in the paper already: queries where extraction fails entirely (temporal accuracy, supersession) fall back to baseline and show no improvement, so the +45pp demonstrably comes from the ranking mechanism applied on top of existing links, not from labels rewarding extraction success. The residual risk is narrower than stated: it's whether the ss-position component of the method and the 'primary entity' component of the label rule jointly favor subject-initial facts. That is a real but narrower confound (about-labeling vs. position-heuristic), better addressed by the two-rater rubric suggestion than by calling the whole ground truth circular. Severity major, not critical; the fix is procedural and cheap.
cross_challenges.evidence: Finding 1: 'packy (1→10), memory_hub (2→10), fuseeval (2→10), Memory Court (1→10). On queries where extraction fails, entity-aware retrieval correctly falls back to the baseline.' Table tab:coverage: Memory Court 4.7% coverage, temporal accuracy 0%. Analysis: fallback queries (supersession, temporal accuracy, MEMORY.md) account for the remaining errors, i.e., they contribute baseline-level precision, confirming the gain is not from extraction success.

data.agreement_note: I fully agree with E1-N01 (the 28 vs 19/100 discrepancy, the unexplained second pass, and the ±2/10 rerun variance on supersession make the headline number unreconstructable — this alone justifies rejection until the 100 labeled pairs and pass provenance are published) and E1-N05 (the 30/80/200 thresholds, the ≥3-fact gate, and 0.7/0.2/0.1 weights are five free constants evaluated on n=10, with no sensitivity analysis or held-out queries, and the character-vs-byte ambiguity for Chinese text is a genuine portability defect). E1-N04's request for a 'extractor ran vs never ran' audit is sound; I'd add that the '4,136 links from 4 patterns on 827 facts (~5/fact)' figure, combined with 'net effect neutral', is itself evidence of over-extraction and undercuts the enhanced-index claim. My challenges are about severity calibration and causal framing on N03 and N02, not about their factual content; N01 remains the paper's fatal flaw.
